mstts:express-as.prosody: As we wrap up, let’s bring together the big ideas we’ve uncovered. Commodities aren’t just things—they have a double life: there’s what they’re useful for, and what they’re worth in exchange, all rooted in the work people put in. Money steps in and changes the game, making it possible for profit to be the driving force, and opening the door for surplus value to be drawn out. The wage system? It hides a deeper reality. Surplus labor gets pulled from workers, and that’s where exploitation quietly happens. All the while, the need to accumulate capital pushes businesses to innovate, compete, and—every so often—face intense crises. Things like class struggle, new technologies, and even unemployment aren’t flukes. They’re baked right into how the system works. And if you look all the way back, you’ll find that both early and ongoing dispossession have always fueled how this system starts and grows. Capitalism keeps itself going through a mix of economic moves, social habits, and the stories we tell ourselves about how things should be. But there’s tension at its core. All these contradictions bring real pain, but they also hold the spark of change. So, what does this all mean for you? When you step back and look at the big picture, you can see capitalism as a living, shifting system—one that shapes not just markets, but daily life itself. Its patterns might seem powerful, but they’re not set in stone. By understanding how value is made, how surplus is taken, and how people’s roles are woven together, you get the power to look past the surface of everyday transactions. And this kind of clarity isn’t just for thinking—it’s a call to action. If all this feels a bit overwhelming, remember: every system is shaped, challenged, and changed by people just like you. The ways we work, trade, and share power aren’t natural laws—they’re choices, built from struggle and history. When you reflect on how these forces play out in your own life, you’re already taking the first step. And when you join with others to imagine something better—to build new ways of working together, with dignity and fairness—real change becomes possible. The first move is to see things clearly. The next is to act, with purpose and hope.
